claim: Daily-reset leveraged/inverse ETFs typically unsuitable for retail investors holding beyond one session; compounding can sharply diverge long-run performance from the stated daily objective, magnified by higher volatility.
quote: inverse and leveraged ETFs that are reset daily typically are unsuitable for retail investors who plan to hold them for longer than one trading session, particularly in volatile markets
market_and_period: US, all daily-reset leveraged/inverse ETFs, general (pre-dates single-stock LETFs, which launched 2022).
applicability: Direct motivation for this iteration's vt40 volatility overlay (down-only exposure cap) and the monthly-not-daily rebalance cadence on the synthetic L2_<SYM> series -- the daily-reset compounding risk this notice describes is exactly what the vol target is meant to bound. Also grounds why this iteration treats the leveraged legs as a mechanism test, not a promotion-eligible standalone holding.
limitations: General leveraged/inverse ETF notice, not specific to single-stock products (which did not exist in 2009) or to a synthetic (non-exchange-traded) 2x series like the one this iteration constructs.
independent_replication: Consistent with this project's own prior local finding on a different leveraged-ETF family: dir:levered_single_asset_sma_trend_gate (registry) found a 40-cell leveraged-trend family voided by a calendar-shift placebo, with an independently-cited -48% 2022 drawdown caveat on a real leveraged-ETF trend strategy.

claim: Alpaca's own margin docs: a Reg T Margin Account holding $10,000 cash may purchase and hold up to $20,000 in marginable securities overnight (2x overnight leverage); margin interest rates are 5.00% (elite) to 6.50% (non-elite) per year, charged only on the end-of-day debit balance; when a single security represents >=70% of equity value in accounts with >=$100,000 margin balance, the maintenance margin rate on that concentrated position rises to 50%.
quote: a Reg T Margin Account holding $10,000 cash may purchase and hold up to $20,000 in marginable securities overnight; 5.00% for elite users and 6.50% for non-elite users
market_and_period: US, Alpaca brokerage margin accounts, current as of fetch.
applicability: Grounds two preregistered choices: (1) a real Alpaca-executed version of this strategy's 2x exposure would be financed via Reg T margin, not a synthetic swap -- the brief's fin_d=2.5%/year financing-spread assumption is deliberately conservative relative to Alpaca's own documented 5.00-6.50% margin rate, recorded here as a caveat, not adjusted in the preregistered formula; (2) the 50% maintenance-margin escalation on >=70%-concentrated positions is a real execution-feasibility constraint on the k=1 (single-name, up to 100% weight before vt40 scaling) candidates that a promotion-stage review would need to re-check.
limitations: Rates and thresholds can change; not independently cross-checked against a second Alpaca source this session.

claim: Quantpedia's 'Momentum Effect in Stocks in Small Portfolios' strategy (10 long / 10 short, 12-month ranking, yearly rebalance): reported CAGR 32% but maximum drawdown -88.09%; the strategy's own out-of-sample backtest cut shows performance deteriorating (slightly negative), moderating confidence in the anomaly's post-publication persistence.
quote: CAGR: 32% annualized return; Maximum Drawdown: -88.09%; The out-of-sample backtest showed slightly negative performance
market_and_period: US equities, long-short 10/10 concentrated momentum, multi-decade backtest with a stated OOS cut.
applicability: Direct quantitative evidence that concentrating momentum into a small basket (here, 10 names one side) produces a Sharpe-flattering headline return alongside tail risk far beyond this project's G1 max-drawdown gate (-35%), and that the effect has decayed out of sample -- both cited as the reason this iteration relies on the vt40 overlay and reports max drawdown explicitly for every candidate rather than judging on CAGR alone.
limitations: Long-short 10/10, not long-only top-1/2/3 out of a megacap-liquidity menu as this iteration tests; no cost assumption stated; not leveraged.
independent_replication: Directionally consistent with this project's own local negative result dir:equity_momentum_concentrated_pwb (top-37 concentrated momentum on the broad top-500 universe: anchor Sharpe 1.03 vs 1.19 bar, stress 0.51 vs 0.65 bar -- both K1 and K2 failed).

claim: Daniel & Moskowitz (2016), 'Momentum Crashes', Journal of Financial Economics 122(2):221-247: momentum strategies have strong positive average returns but experience infrequent, forecastable 'crash' clusters of large negative returns, occurring in panic states (following market declines, when volatility is high) and contemporaneous with market rebounds -- consistent with a conditionally high premium on the option-like payoff of past losers.
quote: momentum strategies can experience infrequent and persistent strings of negative returns...they occur in panic states...and are contemporaneous with market rebounds
market_and_period: US equities, long-short momentum, 1927-2013 (NBER working paper / published JFE version).
applicability: Peer-reviewed academic grounding for the tail-risk mechanism this iteration's placebo and vt40 overlay are meant to probe -- a concentrated, leveraged momentum book is a magnified version of exactly the crash-prone payoff this paper documents, motivating the explicit max-drawdown and stress-window reporting (not just anchor-window Sharpe) for every candidate.
limitations: Long-short, broad-universe academic factor construction, not a long-only top-1/2/3 megacap-menu book; not leveraged; not this project's specific cost/fill convention.
independent_replication: Consistent with the local registry: dir:momentum_risk_control_vs_spmo (refuted, cited by dir:levered_single_asset_sma_trend_gate) found the raw momentum book's drawdown profile could not be fixed without giving up most of the excess return.

claim: Piras, 'Concentrated Portfolios of Momentum Stocks' (SSRN 3695892): a long-only sector-neutral 10-stock momentum sub-portfolio book gained 11.3%/yr, Sharpe 0.59 (vs MSCI USA 6.00%/0.24) over a 20-year sample. Using 1000 random subsampled universes, Piras finds a statistically significant monotonic relation between fewer stocks and higher performance, but also that concentrated (<10 stock) portfolio results show clear dependency on the specific universe constituents chosen -- i.e. the concentration effect is real on average but individual realizations are noisy/universe-sensitive.
quote: a long only portfolio based on overlapping sector neutral sub-portfolios with 10 stocks each, gained an annualized return of 11.3% with a Sharpe ratio of 0.59...portfolios with less than 10 stocks[] show clear dependency on the given universe constituents
market_and_period: US equities, long-only sector-neutral momentum, 10-stock and sub-10-stock concentrated portfolios, ~20-year sample.
applicability: Directly on-topic academic evidence for the core question (does concentrating momentum into 1-3 names help or hurt risk-adjusted return): supports that concentration CAN raise average Sharpe modestly (0.59 vs 0.38 equal-weighted benchmark at n=10, sector-neutral) but explicitly warns that going below 10 names makes results universe-dependent/noisy -- directly relevant caution for this iteration's k in {1,2,3} cells, and part of the reason a random-pick placebo and an equal-weight-no-picking control are preregistered rather than judging the best k-cell alone.
limitations: SSRN full text is paywalled/bot-blocked (curl and WebFetch both returned 403); this claim is built from a WebSearch snippet summary, not the read primary text. Sector-neutral, not megacap-liquidity-menu; not leveraged; no live/paper track record.
independent_replication: Same direction (concentration raises average return, adds dispersion risk) as quantpedia_momentum_small_portfolios_88pct_drawdown and this project's own dir:equity_momentum_concentrated_pwb local result.

claim: 'Beyond Volatility Decay: Correcting Relative Expected Return Estimates for Leveraged Exchange Traded Funds' (MDPI Journal of Risk and Financial Management, 2025-12): the standard method LETF providers use to disclose long-run expected returns relative to the underlying index produces estimates that significantly deviate from statistically correct values; current methods underestimate bullish LETF expected returns by over 100 percentage points/year in high-return/high-volatility regimes (and equally overstate bearish LETF performance in negative-return/low-volatility regimes), with the error magnified at higher leverage.
quote: Current methods underestimate LETF expected returns by over one hundred percentage points annually for bullish LETFs during high-return/high-volatility environments...these errors are magnified with higher leverage
market_and_period: General leveraged ETF structure, methodology paper (not asset- or period-specific backtest).
applicability: Peer-reviewed grounding that naive daily-reset leverage return/vol estimates (including the synthetic 2x series this iteration constructs) can materially mis-state true long-run expected return once realized volatility regime is accounted for -- reinforces why every candidate's reported number is the actual simulated backtest output (not a formula-based 2x scaling of the 1x book), and why the vt40 overlay (bounding realized vol, not just capping notional leverage) is the risk control this iteration relies on.
limitations: WebFetch on the MDPI page returned 403; this claim is built from a WebSearch snippet summary, not the read full text. General LETF methodology, not single-stock-specific.
independent_replication: Consistent in direction with finra_notice_09_31_leveraged_reset_unsuitable's compounding-risk illustration.

claim: SEC Commissioner Crenshaw's 2022-07-11 public statement on single-stock ETFs raised investor-protection concerns ahead of the first single-stock leveraged/inverse ETF launches: daily-reset leverage on a single name compounds both the underlying stock's own idiosyncratic volatility and the fund's structural leverage decay, a materially different risk profile from index-level leveraged ETFs.
quote: Just in 2022, the first single-stock leveraged ETF was launched. Single stock ETFs are some of the poorest performers in a leveraged ETF structure, due to the fact that single stocks are generally more volatile than indexes, hence creating more volatility drag.
market_and_period: US, single-stock leveraged/inverse ETF product category, launched 2022 onward.
applicability: Direct regulator-level caution specific to the single-stock-leverage mechanism this iteration synthesizes (not sector/index leverage, which S3 already uses) -- motivates keeping every candidate's universe restricted to the liquid megacap menu (not extending to smaller/more volatile names) and treating any keep-tier result as a research finding, not a paper-readiness signal (paper activation is out of scope for this iteration regardless of result).
limitations: A policy statement, not an empirical study; the volatility-drag claim in the summary is asserted, not independently derived from a specific dataset in the statement itself.

Two independently-cited real-world leveraged-strategy write-ups add period bias / no-costs and a documented -48% 2022 drawdown (with the intended TLT hedge breaking exactly when needed) as their own honest caveats.
quote: a calendar-shift placebo...beat the real gate in 100% of seeds in the holdout window...Entire 40-cell leveraged-trend family voided
market_and_period: US leveraged single-asset ETFs (index-level, not single-stock), SMA trend-gate mechanism, this project's own frozen windows/cost contract.
applicability: Adjacent negative evidence on a different mechanism (trend-following gate, not momentum stock-picking) applied to leveraged single-asset instruments -- the common thread with this iteration is that leveraged single-name/single-asset exposure looks strong on a raw backtest but has repeatedly failed this project's own placebo tests. Cited as the reason this iteration preregisters both an equal-weight-no-picking control AND a random-pick placebo (not just a calendar-shift placebo), so a positive result cannot survive on leverage/vol-target mechanics alone.
limitations: Different mechanism (SMA trend gate vs 63-day momentum ranking) and different instruments (existing 3x/2x index ETFs vs this iteration's synthetic 2x single-stock series).
